claims.text: Gluten-free rice noodles are available as a substitute for the standard wheat ramen noodles (some noodle swaps carry a small fee). One reviewer specifically described ordering 'tantan ramen with soy meat and rice noodles (gluten free noodles).'
The shop also notes gluten-free options on its menu and offers gluten-free cakes, indicating real awareness of gluten-free diners.

No information is documented about a dedicated gluten-free cooking station, separate noodle-boiling water, or cross-contamination protocols, so strict celiac diners should confirm equipment handling directly with staff.

Unlike most ramen shops, Towzen states it uses gluten-free soy sauce, which it boils down (along with mirin) to reduce alcohol content below 0.1%. This addresses the usual wheat-in-soy-sauce concern that makes most ramen broths unsafe for celiacs.
The kitchen has been fully vegan (100% plant-based) since 2018, with broth built on organic soy milk rather than meat or fish stock — so there is no cross-contact with animal products.
The cooking follows shōjin ryōri principles, prepared without animal products or alliums (onion/garlic), which also makes it suitable for stricter Buddhist and oriental-vegan diners.
Orders are highly customizable — diners can choose flavor, spice level, portion size and noodle type, and reviewers note staff speak good English, making it easier to communicate dietary needs.
The menu lists oriental-vegan, halal and gluten-free options, showing the staff routinely accommodate dietary requests.
Fully vegan kitchen with no animal-product cross-contact — a rare confident choice for plant-based diners.

Genuine gluten-free pathway: gluten-free rice noodles plus gluten-free soy sauce, which is unusual for a ramen shop. Celiac diners should still confirm noodle-boiling and shared-equipment handling in person.

This is a busy conveyor-belt sushi shop where many different dishes — including breaded, fried, and wheat-based items like ramen and rolls — share the same kitchen, conveyor, and shared equipment. That makes meaningful cross-contact with wheat very likely, so it should not be considered celiac-safe.

Standard Japanese soy sauce (shoyu) almost always contains wheat, and the table/conveyor soy sauce at conveyor-belt sushi chains is conventional shoyu. Plain nigiri may look gluten-free, but the soy sauce typically is not — bring your own certified gluten-free tamari if you are celiac.

A handful of items (such as inari, cucumber rolls, certain sides and desserts) may appear plant-based, but everything rides a shared conveyor and is prepared in a fish- and seafood-heavy kitchen, so cross-contact with fish, shellfish, and egg is expected. Sauces and broths frequently use dashi (fish stock). Confirm ingredients item by item.

Sushiro publishes chain-wide allergen information for its menu items, which can help identify which dishes contain major allergens; however, no location-specific allergy-handling practices for the Gion branch were found, so confirm directly with staff before ordering.
The menu and ordering are touch-panel based with published chain-wide allergen charts, so you can look up listed allergens for individual items before ordering.
As a slightly off-center Gion location, it can be calmer than the busiest downtown shops, which may make it easier to take time and ask questions about ingredients.

Falafel is deep-fried, and the menu also serves wheat-based pita and fried sides (fries) in the same kitchen. No source describes a separate fryer or dedicated gluten-free prep area, so cross-contamination in the oil and on shared surfaces should be assumed possible. Falafel, hummus, and salads are naturally gluten-free by recipe, but the pita is not — celiac diners should confirm fry-oil separation with staff before ordering.

This is Middle Eastern / Israeli cooking (falafel, hummus, kebab, tahini-based sauces) rather than Japanese cuisine, so wheat-containing Japanese soy sauce is not a typical ingredient. No source confirms an entirely soy-free or wheat-free sauce lineup, so anyone highly sensitive should still verify sauces directly.

The restaurant openly serves vegetarian, vegan, and omnivore diners side by side, with vegan items clearly marked on the menu and pita sandwiches described as well suited to vegans. Chicken kebab is cooked in the same kitchen, so strict vegans concerned about shared grills or utensils should ask, but the place is set up to handle plant-based orders.

One source notes the menu offers egg-free, milk-free, wheat-free, and 'allergen-free' options and marks vegan dishes clearly, suggesting staff are accustomed to dietary requests. This is a menu-labeling claim, not a verified allergen-control protocol, so celiac and severe-allergy diners should still confirm specifics in person.
Cooks without chemical seasonings and emphasizes additive- and pesticide-free ingredients, with vegan dishes clearly labeled on the menu.
The owner speaks fluent English and there is a picture menu, which makes discussing dietary needs and allergies much easier for international diners.
Core dishes — falafel, hummus, baba ganoush, and vegetable-packed salads/pita fillings — are naturally plant-based and, apart from the wheat pita, naturally gluten-free by recipe.

The owner can accommodate gluten-free diners when given about a day's notice ahead of your visit, since she cooks everything herself and can plan around it. No dedicated gluten-free prep area or formal cross-contamination protocol is documented, so celiac diners should confirm details directly when they call to arrange it.

No information is available on whether the soy sauce used is wheat-free. Most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, and tempeh/teriyaki and miso-based dishes here may involve it, so celiac diners should ask specifically about the soy sauce and seasonings when arranging a gluten-free meal.
The kitchen is fully plant-based, so animal-product cross-contact is not a concern; there is no meat, fish, dairy, or egg cooking on site to mix with vegan dishes.
The owner cooks all dishes herself and speaks English, and reviewers note she explains menu items to non-Japanese guests, which makes it easy to discuss ingredients and allergies in person.
Entirely vegan menu, so plant-based diners can order anything without worrying about hidden animal products.
Strong emphasis on organic and pesticide-free vegetables and pesticide-free rice, reflecting the owner's focus on safe, trustworthy ingredients.
A single owner-cook who handles the whole kitchen and speaks English makes it straightforward to communicate dietary needs and arrange gluten-free meals in advance.

No specific reports about fryer sharing or cross-contamination in the kitchen were found, so celiac diners should confirm directly with the owner. Note that several signature items are not gluten-free as served - pita bread is wheat, and sabich and shawarma are typically served in or with pita.

This is Israeli cooking built on spices, vegetables and olive oil rather than Japanese soy-sauce or dashi bases, so wheat-containing soy sauce is far less likely to appear than in a typical Japanese eatery - but no source confirms the seasonings used, so confirm with staff if you are strictly avoiding wheat.

The kitchen serves meat dishes (shawarma, meat hummus) alongside vegan items, and no source describes how preparation is separated, so vegan diners avoiding all animal contact should ask the owner how dishes are cooked.
The owner Moshe is hands-on, speaks fluent Japanese and English, and the menu is multilingual, which makes it easy to discuss ingredients and dietary needs in person.

Naturally strong for plant-based diners: the menu explicitly recommends its healthy, satisfying vegetable dishes for vegan and vegetarian guests, and staples like hummus, falafel, baba ganoush and salads are vegetable-forward.
The listing notes that vegan, vegetarian, gluten-free and kosher options are offered, so there is room to ask for accommodations.

name: Kyoto Wagyu Steak Sandwich Pizza (Halal/Vegan/GF) – Kiyomizu

claims.text: This is a Wagyu steak, sandwich, pizza, burger and ramen house — an environment built around wheat (bread, pizza dough, ramen, breading) and shared cooking surfaces. Gluten-free items are advertised, but no source confirms a separated gluten-free prep area or how cross-contact is controlled, so celiac diners should not assume it is celiac-safe and should confirm in person.

Wagyu, ramen and burger dishes here are typically seasoned with Japanese-style sauces, and most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat. No source specifies whether a wheat-free/tamari soy sauce is used, so anyone strictly avoiding gluten should ask which sauces and seasonings are wheat-free.

Vegan options are advertised, and the group is known to offer a vegetarian tofu-based burger, but this is primarily a Wagyu beef kitchen where vegan items are likely cooked alongside meat. No source describes separate utensils or surfaces for vegan dishes, so cross-contact with beef should be assumed unless staff confirm otherwise.
The restaurant openly advertises halal, vegan and gluten-free options and is set up to accommodate travelers with varied dietary needs, so staff are accustomed to such requests.
The Wagyu is sourced halal, and the group offers gluten-free buns and a plant-based/tofu burger alternative, giving GF and vegan diners a starting point to discuss with staff.

This is not a celiac-safe restaurant. Fresh wheat gluten (namafu) is a central, recurring ingredient in the shojin-ryori course - it appears sliced, molded into plum-blossom shapes, and inside dumplings across multiple courses.

A detailed course documented multiple gluten-containing dishes (fresh gluten with soy sauce, fresh gluten plum blossom, kenchin-maki dumplings wrapped in fried yuba), confirming wheat is woven throughout the meal rather than confined to one dish.

Soy sauce seasons several dishes and a white (saikyo) miso soup anchors a course; both standard Japanese soy sauce and miso typically contain wheat, adding further gluten exposure on top of the namafu.

The cooking follows strict Buddhist precepts - no meat, dairy, eggs or pungent alliums - and the broths are vegetable-based, so the menu is fully plant-based by design. Reviewers consistently describe the meals as entirely vegan with no animal products.
The sesame 'tofu' is made from kuzu (arrowroot) starch and ground sesame rather than soybeans, and the kenchin dumpling is served in a vegetable dashi (no bonito/fish stock).

Reviewers describe the kimono-clad family hosts as extremely accommodating and willing to explain how to eat each dish, though English is limited; no reviewer documented how the kitchen handles specific allergies.
Fully vegan, multi-course Buddhist temple cuisine - a reliable choice for plant-based diners avoiding meat, fish, dairy, eggs and alliums.
Cooked entirely by family members with no outside staff, with reservations required - a setting where you can speak directly with the hosts about your needs when booking.

MOS offers a 'low allergen' line — a pork rice-burger and a pork hot dog, both on rice-flour buns — that is certified free of wheat, egg, milk, shrimp, crab, peanut, and buckwheat, and served in sealed individual packaging to limit cross-contact. These items are children's-size and small, so celiac diners often order two.

MOS states its allergen information reflects product ingredients only, and that ingredients not normally used in an item may be introduced through contact or mixing during factory manufacturing or in-store cooking — so the allergen list is not an absolute guarantee.

MOS notes that in-store kitchens use the same standard cooking equipment and utensils and also prepare other products, meaning shared-surface cross-contact is possible for anything not in the sealed low-allergen packaging.

Standard menu items such as the Teriyaki Burger use sauces that typically contain wheat-based soy sauce, so popular non-low-allergen items are not wheat-free. Rely only on the certified low-allergen items and the published allergen chart for a strictly gluten-free order.

This is an omnivore burger shop with no documented dedicated vegan menu at this branch. MOS does offer plant-based 'Green' burgers chain-wide, but they are cooked on shared equipment alongside meat and dairy items, so cross-contact is likely — confirm specifics with staff.
An allergen chart is available in English on the MOS website (downloadable PDF), and the company directs customers with allergy concerns to check the list and ask store staff directly.

The certified low-allergen pork rice-burger and pork hot dog are free of wheat, egg, milk, shrimp, crab, peanut, and buckwheat and arrive in sealed packaging — a rare, genuinely usable option for celiac diners at a Japanese burger chain.
An English-language allergen chart is published online, making it easier to verify ingredients before ordering.
Every item is made to order rather than pre-assembled, so you can speak with staff about your order at the counter when you place it.
